passages.title: The Kickflip
sentences: Leo wanted to land a kickflip.
He tried ten times at the skate park.
He fell off each time.
He sat on the ramp and frowned.
Then he got up and tried again.
This time, his feet came down on the board.
He rolled all the way to the end.
Leo threw his arms up and grinned.
"I did it!" he yelled.

passages.title: The Rock Club
sentences: On Tuesday, Maya went to the new rock club at the library.
All the other kids were new to her.
They sat in pairs and talked and laughed.
Maya sat at the end of the long table by herself.
She looked down at her rock and turned it in her hands.
The room was full of kids, but Maya felt alone.
Then a girl with a robot pin sat down next to her.
It was Priya.
"Is that quartz?" Priya asked.
Maya looked up and smiled.
"Yes," she said. "I found it by the creek."

passages.title: Earth from Space
sentences: Astronauts live and work on a space station high above Earth.
The station goes all the way around Earth in about ninety minutes.
From a big window, they can see the whole curve of the planet.
They see blue oceans, white clouds and brown sand.
At night, they see the lights of cities as tiny dots.
Many astronauts say they stare out the window for a long time.
They say Earth looks small and lovely at the same time.
They feel amazed.
This big, quiet, amazed feeling has a name.
It is called wonder.

passages.title: Storm Night
sentences: Sam was staying the night at Grandma Rose's house above the bakery.
After dinner, dark clouds came in from the sea.
Soon, rain hit the windows hard.
A flash of light filled the room, and then thunder boomed.
Pixel ran under the bed and shook.
Sam's heart beat fast.
He pulled the blanket up to his chin.
Grandma Rose came in and sat on the end of the bed.
"Storms are loud, but this house is strong and safe," she said.
"Let's count from the flash to the boom."
At the next flash, they counted to five before the boom.
Each time, the count got longer.
"That means the storm is moving away," said Grandma Rose.
Sam took slow breaths.
His hands felt warm and still.
Pixel came out and curled up by his feet.
Soon the only sound was soft rain, and Sam fell asleep.

passages.title: The Last Match
sentences: On Saturday, the Harbor Hawks played the last soccer match of the year.
Ana and Ben were both on the team.
The score was one to one, with two minutes left.
Ben passed the ball to Ana.
Ana ran past two players and kicked the ball as hard as she could.
It flew into the top corner of the net.
The whistle blew, and the Hawks had won.
Ana jumped up and down, and the whole team ran to hug her.
On the bus ride home, Ana smiled at the window.
At dinner, she told the story of the goal three times.
That night, she put her muddy ball on the shelf next to her bed.

passages.title: Ana's Trumpet Solo
sentences: On Thursday night, the Grade 6 band and the Grade 7 band played their first concert of the year.
Ana had a short trumpet solo in the very last song.
She had practiced it every day after school for a whole month.
Before the show, her hands felt cold, and she kept checking her sheet music.
Then the lights went down, and the band began to play.
When her solo came, Ana stood up and lifted her trumpet.
The first note came out clear and strong.
She played every note exactly the way she had practiced it.
When she sat down, the whole audience clapped, and Ben whistled from the third row.
After the concert, Ana held her trumpet case tight and smiled at everyone she passed.
"I played the whole solo without one mistake," she told her mom.
On the drive home, she hummed the tune of her solo again and again.

passages.title: Dolphins by the Ferry
sentences: On Sunday morning, Sam and Maya took the ferry to Gull Island.
Maya sat by the rail with her sketchbook open on her knees.
Halfway across the bay, she saw a gray fin rise out of the water.
Then she saw another fin, and then five more.
A group of dolphins was swimming right beside the ferry.
They leaped out of the waves in smooth curves and slid back into the sea.
Maya put down her pencil and stood very still.
Her mouth opened, but she did not say a word.
She watched the dolphins until they turned and swam out of sight.
Then she turned to Sam and asked question after question.
"How do they swim so fast? Do they ever sleep? Where are they going?"
Sam did not know the answers, so they planned to find a book about dolphins at the library.
That night, Maya drew the dolphins across a whole page of her sketchbook.

passages.title: The Fox and the Crow
sentences: One morning, a crow spotted a piece of cheese on a windowsill outside a farmhouse kitchen.
She snatched it in her beak and flew up to the highest branch of a tall oak tree.
There she settled comfortably, very pleased with herself, to enjoy her delicious breakfast in peace.
A hungry fox was trotting along the path below, and he noticed the cheese at once.
He sat down beneath the tree and gazed up at the crow with a friendly, admiring smile.
"Good morning, beautiful bird," he called.
"Your feathers shine in the sunlight, and your eyes are bright and clever."
"A bird so lovely must have a lovely voice as well."
"If you would sing just one song for me, I would call you the queen of all the birds."
The crow puffed out her chest and lifted her head high.
Nobody had ever praised her like this before, and she wanted the fox to hear her voice.
She opened her beak wide and gave the loudest caw she could.
At that very moment, the cheese slipped out of her beak and tumbled down to the ground.
The fox snapped it up and gulped it down in one bite.
"Thank you for breakfast," said the fox, licking his whiskers.
"In return, here is some advice: be careful of anyone who praises you only to get something from you."
Then he trotted away down the path.
The crow sat on her branch with an empty beak, and her feathers drooped.
She wished, more than anything, that she had kept her beak shut.

credit.title: The Fox and the Crow
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Night Train
sentences: Sam had wanted to ride a sleeper train for years, and in July he finally got his chance.
He and Grandma Rose were taking the overnight train to visit his uncle in a city far to the north.
The night before, Sam spread his paper map across the kitchen table and traced the route with a green pen.
He counted eleven stations between Harbor Town and the city.
At the station, he read every line on the departure board twice, and he could not keep his feet still.
Their sleeping compartment was tiny, with two narrow beds, one above the other.
For the first few hours, Sam sat by the window and checked off each station on his map.
Then the sky grew dark, and Grandma Rose fell asleep in the lower bed.
Sam climbed into the top bed, but he could not fall asleep.
The train rocked and clicked, and the little room felt strange and much too quiet.
He thought about Pixel curled up at the end of his own bed, far away at home.
He wished that someone were awake to talk to.
Near dawn, a soft gray light came in around the edges of the blind, and Sam lifted it.
The train was crossing a high bridge over a wide valley.
Far below, a river curved between dark green hills, and mist floated above the water.
In the distance, the snowy tops of the mountains were turning pink in the first sunlight.
Sam held his breath and did not move until the bridge was behind them.
Then he found the river on his map and marked the bridge with a small star.
When Grandma Rose woke up, he showed her the star and said, "That was the best part of the whole trip."

passages.title: The Bone in the Hill
sentences: Paleontologists are scientists who study fossils, the remains of plants and animals that lived long ago.
Many of them spend their summers in badlands, which are areas of dry, rocky hills with very few plants.
In the badlands, wind and rain slowly wear away the rock, and ancient bones are sometimes uncovered at the surface.
One paleontologist searches the same badlands for six weeks every summer.
Most days, she walks for hours with her eyes on the ground and finds nothing but broken stones and dust.
One hot afternoon, late in her third week, she noticed a dark brown shape poking out of a gray slope.
It had a smooth, curved surface, and its color was different from the rocks around it.
She knelt down and brushed away the dust with her fingers.
Her heart began to pound, because she recognized what it was: the rounded end of a very large bone.
Over the next ten days, her team uncovered the bone slowly, using small picks, dental tools and soft brushes.
They could not hurry, because a fossil can crack if it is handled roughly.
Over many hours, a thigh bone longer than a grown person's leg appeared from the rock.
The team believed it came from a large plant-eating dinosaur that lived about seventy million years ago.
To protect it for the journey, they wrapped it in strips of cloth dipped in wet plaster, much like a cast for a broken arm.
On the last day, the team lifted the heavy plaster jacket into the back of a truck.
Before she left, the paleontologist sat on the slope and looked out over the silent hills.
No person had ever seen that bone before her team found it.
For millions of years, it had lain hidden under the ground, and soon it would rest in a museum where thousands of visitors could see it.
She smiled, wiped the dust from her hands and wrote the date in her field notebook.
Years later, she still told her students that touching that bone was the best moment of her career.

passages.title: Waiting for the Rover
sentences: After a journey of about seven months through space, a rover was finally about to land on Mars.
The rover was a robot about the size of a small car, with six wheels, many cameras and a long arm for studying rocks.
Hundreds of engineers had spent years designing and building it.
One of them had worked on its wheels for five years, testing them again and again on sand and sharp stones.
Landing on Mars is very difficult, because the rover arrives many times faster than a jet plane.
In about seven minutes, it must slow down almost to a stop, using a heat shield, a huge parachute and small rockets.
Nobody on Earth can steer it during those minutes.
On landing day, a radio signal from Mars took more than ten minutes to reach Earth.
So by the time the team heard that the landing had begun, it was already over, and all they could do was wait for the news.
In the control room, the wheel engineer sat at his desk and stared at the screens.
His hands were cold, and he kept tapping his foot on the floor.
A voice read out each message as it arrived: the heat shield, the parachute, the rockets.
Then came the words the whole room had been waiting for: "Touchdown confirmed."
The room filled with cheers, and the engineer jumped up and hugged the people next to him.
He laughed, and at the same time his eyes filled with tears.
A few minutes later, the first picture from the rover appeared on the big screen.
It was grainy and black and white, and it showed only dusty ground and a few small rocks.
To the team, it looked more beautiful than any picture they had ever seen.
The engineer leaned close to the screen and thought about the six wheels he had helped to build, now resting on the ground of another planet.

passages.title: First Snow
sentences: Sam woke up early on Saturday.
His room was very quiet, and the light looked white.
He pulled back the curtain.
Snow covered the street, the cars and the trees.
It was the first snow of the winter.
Sam pulled on his boots and coat as fast as he could.
Pixel ran to the front door and spun in a circle.
Outside, Pixel jumped into the snow and rolled on his back.
Sam laughed so hard that he fell down too.
They ran up and down the street until their noses were cold.
Then Sam lay on his back and let the flakes land on his face.

passages.title: The Turtle Walk
sentences: Sea turtles lay their eggs in the sand on warm beaches.
About two months later, the baby turtles hatch.
They dig out of the sand together, most often at night.
Then the babies crawl as fast as they can toward the sea.
They go toward the brightest part of the sky, which is over the water.
That is why some beach towns ask people to turn off their lights at night.
People who come to watch keep their lights off and stand very still.
When a wave lifts a tiny turtle away, many of them smile and whisper.
Some say it was the best night of their whole year.

passages.title: The Leap at Rhodes
sentences: Long ago, a young athlete came home after a long trip across the sea.
Every day, he stood in the town square and told stories about himself.
"On the island of Rhodes, I made the longest jump anyone has ever seen," he said.
"The crowd cheered, and the judges gave me a prize."
"If you ever go to Rhodes, ask the people there. They will tell you."
He held his head high and smiled at everyone who walked by.
After many days, the people in the square grew tired of the same story.
At last, an old man stepped forward and drew a line in the dust with his stick.
"We do not need to go to Rhodes," he said kindly.
"Let us pretend this square is Rhodes. Show us your jump right here."
The athlete looked down at the line in the dust.
His face turned red, and he did not say another word.
Then he walked away, and the people went back to their work.

credit.title: The Leap at Rhodes
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Map Walk
sentences: On Thursday, Ms. Ortiz took her science class to Story Woods for a map walk.
Each group received a paper map with five red dots on it.
Each dot marked the place where an orange flag was hidden.
Sam, Priya and Leo were in one group.
At the first fork in the trail, Leo started to run down the left path.
Sam turned the map until it matched the trail, and then he located the creek on it.
"The creek should be on our right," he said. "We need the other path."
They followed the path to the right, and soon they discovered the first flag beside the creek.
After that, Leo and Priya waited for Sam at every fork.
They collected all five flags before lunch.
Back at the bus, Ms. Ortiz asked which person had read the map.
Priya and Leo both pointed at Sam.
Sam stood up straight, and he held the map against his chest all the way home.

passages.title: One Player
sentences: Ana was away at band camp for a whole week.
On Monday, Ben turned on the game that the twins always played together.
It was a game for two players, and the second controller sat on the couch.
Ben played one level by himself, and then he turned the game off.
The house felt much too quiet without Ana's loud laugh.
He went to his room and lay on his bed, looking at the ceiling.
On Tuesday, Leo knocked on the door with his skateboard under his arm.
"Do you want to go to the skate park?" Leo asked.
Ben shook his head and pointed at the game.
"I need a second player," he said.
Leo had never played the game before, but he picked up the controller.
Ben showed him how to jump and how to build a bridge.
By dinner time, they had beaten three levels, and Ben was laughing again.

passages.title: Sam's First Loaves
sentences: On Saturday, Sam got up at five in the morning to help at Rose's Bakery.
Grandma Rose showed him how to mix flour, water, salt and yeast.
Then he pushed and folded the dough for ten whole minutes.
His arms got tired, but he did not stop.
The dough rested in a warm place and grew to twice its size.
Sam shaped it into four round loaves, and Grandma Rose slid them into the hot oven.
Soon the whole bakery smelled warm and sweet.
The loaves came out golden brown and crackly on top.
At eight o'clock, the first customer bought one of Sam's loaves.
Sam watched her carry it out the door.
He could not stop smiling for the rest of the morning.
When Mrs. Lin came in for her café order, Sam pointed at the shelf.
"The round ones are mine," he said. "I made them myself."

passages.title: Above the Clouds
sentences: On Sunday morning, Maya and Priya hiked up to the lookout on Lantern Peaks.
Maya wanted to draw the view of Harbor Town from the top.
But when they got there, thick fog was all around them.
They could not even see the trees ten steps away.
Maya sat on a rock and closed her sketchbook with a sigh.
"We walked all this way for nothing," she said.
Priya poured her a cup of hot cocoa, and they waited.
After half an hour, the fog began to sink down the hill.
Then the sun came through, and both girls gasped.
They were above the clouds.
Below them, the whole valley was filled with white cloud.
Only the tops of the hills stuck out, dark green in the bright sun.
Maya opened her sketchbook again, and she did not say a word for a long time.

passages.title: Looking Up
sentences: I lie on my back in the cool, wet grass.
The sky is black, and the stars come out one by one.
First there are ten, then a hundred, and then too many to count.
A pale band of light stretches across the whole sky.
It is the Milky Way, the enormous galaxy that is our home.
Some of that light left its star before I was born.
I feel very small under so much sky.
But being small does not make me sad.
I feel wide awake, and I have so many questions.
How far away is the farthest star?
Is someone on another planet looking up at me?
I stay outside until my mom calls me in.
Even then, I leave my window open, so I can still see the sky.

passages.title: The Ant and the Dove
sentences: On a hot summer afternoon, a thirsty ant climbed down to the edge of a stream to drink.
As she leaned over the water, a gust of wind knocked her off the bank.
The current swept her away from the shore, and she kicked her tiny legs as hard as she could.
Her heart raced, and no matter how hard she kicked, she could not reach the bank.
A dove was resting on a branch that hung over the stream, and she saw the ant struggling.
Quickly, the dove pulled a leaf from the branch with her beak and dropped it into the water beside the ant.
The ant scrambled onto the leaf and clung to it while it drifted slowly toward the shore.
When she finally stepped onto dry ground, she lay still for a long moment.
Then she looked up at the dove and called out her thanks.
A few days later, a bird catcher crept up to the same tree, carrying a large net.
He was watching the dove, but the dove had not noticed him.
The ant saw him raise the net, and she knew she had to act.
She was tiny, and the man was enormous, but she marched straight up to his ankle and bit him as hard as she could.
"Ouch!" he shouted, and he dropped the net.
The noise startled the dove, and she flew high into the sky, safe and free.
Down in the grass, the ant felt prouder than she had ever felt in her life.

credit.title: The Ant and the Dove
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Peacock and the Crane
sentences: Early one morning, a peacock was strolling through a farmyard when he met a crane.
The peacock was very vain, which means he cared a great deal about how he looked.
To show off, he lifted his enormous tail and spread it wide in the sunshine.
Hundreds of feathers shimmered in green, blue and gold, and each one had a round, shining spot in the middle.
"Look at me," said the peacock, turning slowly so the crane could see every side.
"My feathers have every color of the rainbow, and yours are plain and gray."
The crane did not argue.
He simply stretched out his long, broad wings and leaped into the air.
With a few strong beats, he rose above the barn, then above the trees, and then above the hills.
"Follow me if you can," he called down.
The wind lifted him higher, and he could see the whole valley below him, with its rivers, roads and tiny farms.
He circled slowly in the cool, bright air, enjoying every moment.
Down in the farmyard, the peacock tried to follow.
He flapped and flapped, but his heavy tail dragged behind him, and he only reached the top of the fence.
He stood there for a long time, watching the crane grow smaller and smaller until he was only a dot in the blue sky.
For the first time, his beautiful tail did not make him feel special at all.
Slowly, he folded it up and climbed down from the fence.

credit.title: The Peacock and the Crane
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Glow Room
sentences: On a Saturday in September, Mr. Varga led the rock club into the old tunnel at the mine museum.
The tunnel was cool and damp, and their helmet lamps made small circles of light on the stone walls.
For the first ten minutes, Mr. Varga talked about the iron carts that miners once pushed along the rails.
Maya liked rocks much more than carts, and she kept glancing ahead down the tunnel.
Then Mr. Varga stopped beside a wooden door with a sign that read "Glow Room."
Inside, the room was completely dark, and shelves of gray, dull rocks lined the walls.
"Switch off your lamps," said Mr. Varga, and he pressed a button.
A special lamp filled the room with ultraviolet light, which is mostly invisible to human eyes.
Instantly, the dull rocks glowed in bright colors: green, deep red, orange and electric blue.
Maya stepped closer to the shelves, and for a moment she forgot that anyone else was there.
She had read about glowing minerals in books, but she had never imagined they would be this bright.
"Can anyone name this blue one?" Mr. Varga asked, pointing at a crystal shaped like a cube.
Maya's hand went up before she could think about it.
"Fluorite," she said. "The word fluorescent comes from its name."
"Exactly right," said Mr. Varga, and two older club members turned to look at her.
Maya's cheeks felt warm, but she smiled all the way back up the tunnel.

passages.title: Round Two
sentences: The Harbor Town robot challenge was held in the school gym on a rainy Saturday.
Each team had to drive a small rover through a maze of cardboard walls, pick up a ball and carry it to a box at the end.
Priya had spent six weeks building her rover, and she had tested it every evening in her garage.
When her name was called for round one, she set the rover down at the start line and gripped the controller.
The rover rolled forward smoothly and turned the first corner.
Then, halfway through the maze, it stopped and would not move again.
The buzzer sounded, and Priya carried her rover back to the table without looking at anyone.
Her eyes stung, and she pressed her lips together hard.
Ms. Ortiz sat down beside her and said quietly, "You have twenty minutes before round two."
Priya took three slow breaths, and then she turned the rover over.
One by one, she checked the wheels, the motor and the wires.
At last, she found the problem: a battery wire had come loose when the rover bumped a wall.
She fixed the wire, wrapped it with tape and tested the wheels twice.
In round two, the rover rolled through the whole maze, picked up the ball and dropped it into the box.
Priya finished in third place, not first.
Still, on the drive home, she held the rover on her lap and kept looking at the taped wire.

passages.title: The Fun Run
sentences: Every spring, Harbor Middle School holds a five-kilometer fun run along the harbor path.
Leo had never run that far without stopping, but he signed up anyway.
At the start line, he bounced on his toes and joked with Ana and Ben.
"I'll be finished before you two have tied your shoes," he said, and the twins laughed.
For the first two kilometers, Leo ran fast and easily, passing several other runners.
Then his legs began to feel heavy, and a sharp pain pinched his side.
Runners he had passed earlier jogged past him, one after another.
Leo slowed down, and his jokes stopped completely.
He looked at the long, curving path ahead and thought about walking the rest of the way.
Then he picked one lamppost ahead of him and told himself to reach only that one.
When he reached it, he picked the next lamppost, and then the next.
He crossed the finish line in forty-first place out of sixty runners, red-faced and soaked with sweat.
He had not won, and he had not even finished in the top half.
But for the first time in his life, he had run the whole five kilometers without walking once.
When Ana asked how it went, Leo did not make a joke.
He grinned, held up his finisher's ribbon and said, "I didn't stop. Not even once."

passages.title: The First Solo
sentences: Before a person can earn a pilot's license, they must fly a plane alone for the first time.
This flight is called the first solo.
Student pilots first spend many hours in the air with an instructor, practicing takeoffs, turns and landings.
When the instructor decides that a student is ready, the instructor climbs out, and the student flies alone.
One student pilot still remembers her first solo very clearly.
Her instructor stepped out onto the grass and shut the door, and suddenly the seat beside her was empty.
Her mouth felt dry, and she checked every switch twice before she started down the runway.
Then the small plane lifted into the air, and the ground dropped away beneath her.
Without the instructor's weight, the plane was lighter, and it climbed faster than it ever had before.
She flew one wide loop around the airport, just as she had practiced, and lined up with the runway.
The wheels touched down gently, and she let out a long breath.
Then she did it twice more.
When she climbed out, her instructor was grinning and holding a pair of scissors.
At many flight schools, it is a tradition to cut off the back of a student's shirt after the first solo.
The instructor wrote the date on the piece of shirt, and the student pinned it to the wall at home.
Years later, after hundreds of flights, she still says that no landing has ever felt as good as those first three.

passages.title: The Orchestra
sentences: In March, Ms. Gray took her music students on a bus to the city to hear a full orchestra.
Leo, who played the drums in the Grade 7 band, joked the whole way there.
"Two hours of sitting still," he groaned. "I might fall asleep in my seat."
Priya, who played the cello, could not sit still, and she kept asking Ms. Gray how many cellos there would be.
The concert hall was enormous, with rows of red seats and a ceiling painted gold.
More than eighty musicians walked onto the stage and tuned their instruments.
Then the conductor raised her arms, and the whole hall went silent.
The music began softly, with only the violins, and then it grew louder until Leo could feel it through the floor.
Near the back of the stage, a percussion player struck a pair of huge drums called timpani.
Leo sat forward in his seat, and he did not make a single joke for the rest of the concert.
Priya kept her eyes on the cello section, where ten cellists moved their bows at exactly the same time.
When the cellos played the main tune by themselves, she held her breath until it was over.
On the bus home, Leo talked about nothing except the timpani.
Priya was quiet this time, but she was humming the cello tune very softly, and she was smiling.

passages.title: The Wolf and the House Dog
sentences: One bitter winter evening, at the edge of a forest, a thin, hungry wolf met a well-fed house dog trotting along the road.
The dog's coat was thick and glossy, and his sides were so round that he had clearly never missed a meal in his life.
The wolf had not eaten properly for many days, and he stared at the dog's comfortable body with envy.
Envy is the painful feeling of wanting what someone else has.
"Cousin," said the dog cheerfully, "you look terribly thin. Why do you wander through the cold forest every night, when you could live the way I do?"
"Come and work with me in the village, because my master gives me a full bowl every morning and a warm place beside the fire every evening."
The wolf's ears pricked up as he imagined a full bowl of food waiting for him every single morning, and he licked his lips.
"What work would I have to do?" he asked eagerly.
"Almost nothing," the dog replied, "except barking at strangers and being friendly to the family."
So the two animals set off toward the village side by side, and with every step the wolf walked a little faster.
As they walked, the moon rose, and in its silver light the wolf noticed a bare patch on the dog's neck where the fur had been rubbed away.
"What happened to your neck?" asked the wolf.
"Oh, that is nothing," said the dog, "only where my collar rubs, because my master chains me up every night, but you soon get used to it."
The wolf stopped in the middle of the road.
"A chain?" he said slowly. "Does that mean you cannot always run wherever you like?"
"Not always," admitted the dog, "but what does that matter, when the food is so delicious?"
The wolf looked back at the dark forest, where the wind moved through the tall pines and the first stars were appearing.
"It matters a great deal to me," he answered quietly.
"Good night, cousin, but I would rather be hungry and free than comfortable and chained."
Then he turned and loped back into the forest, and although his stomach was still empty, he ran with his head held high.

credit.title: The Wolf and the House Dog
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Listening to Whales
sentences: Humpback whales are famous for their songs.
Scientists believe that only the males sing, and each song is a long pattern of moans, groans, cries and squeaks.
One song can last from about ten to twenty minutes, and a whale may repeat it again and again for hours.
Even more surprising, all the males in one part of the ocean sing almost the same song, and over many months the song slowly changes as they all change it together.
Scientists still do not know for certain why the whales sing.
To study the songs, researchers lower a hydrophone, which is an underwater microphone, over the side of a boat.
One young researcher spent her first winter on a small boat in warm, clear water where humpbacks gather each year.
For four days, she heard nothing through her headphones except the hiss of the waves and the crackle of tiny shrimp.
Each evening she wrote "no song" in her notebook, and she began to wonder whether she had chosen the wrong career.
On the fifth morning, the captain switched off the engine in a calm bay, and she lowered the hydrophone once more.
At first there was only the familiar hiss.
Then a low, rising moan filled her headphones, so deep that she seemed to feel it as well as hear it.
It was followed by a long cry that climbed higher and higher, and then by a series of short, soft squeaks.
She pressed the headphones against her ears and did not move.
The whale was somewhere below the boat, out of sight, and yet its voice seemed to be all around her.
She listened for almost two hours as the same song came around again and again.
When it finally faded, she realized that her cheeks were wet, although she had not noticed that she was crying.
That evening, she did not write "no song" in her notebook.
Instead, she filled three pages with notes and a long list of questions that she wanted to answer.
Years later, she still keeps that recording, and she plays it whenever she wants to remember why she chose her work.

passages.title: Four Minutes of Night
sentences: A total solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes exactly between the Sun and Earth.
The Sun is about four hundred times wider than the Moon, but it is also about four hundred times farther away, so from Earth the two look almost the same size.
For a few minutes, the Moon can cover the Sun completely, but only for people standing inside a narrow path on the ground.
Because that path is different for every eclipse, many people travel a long way to stand inside it.
On the morning of one eclipse, hundreds of people gathered on a grassy hillside inside the path.
They set up chairs and telescopes, and everyone wore special eclipse glasses, because looking straight at the Sun without them can badly hurt your eyes.
Through the dark glasses, the Sun looked like an orange circle, and slowly a black curve began to cover one side of it.
For more than an hour, the Moon moved across the Sun, and the crowd chatted, ate snacks and checked their cameras.
Then the light began to change.
The sunlight turned thin and silvery, and the air grew noticeably cooler.
The birds in the nearby trees stopped singing.
As the last bright sliver of Sun disappeared, the sky suddenly went dark, and a ring of sunset colors glowed all around the horizon.
People took off their glasses, which is safe only during those minutes of totality, and a gasp went through the whole crowd.
Where the Sun had been, there was a black circle surrounded by pale, feathery light called the corona.
Bright planets appeared in the middle of the day.
For four minutes, almost nobody spoke.
One man stood with his hand over his mouth, and a girl beside him gripped her father's arm and laughed out loud.
Then a flash of sunlight burst from one edge of the Moon, the crowd cheered, and everyone put their glasses back on.
Later, many of them said they could not describe the feeling, and some began planning a trip to the next eclipse that same afternoon.

passages.title: The Long Dark
sentences: At the South Pole, the Sun does not rise and set every day.
Instead, it sets once a year, in March, and it does not rise again until September.
For about six months, the sky is dark, and the temperature outside can drop below minus seventy degrees Celsius.
It is too cold for planes to land, so the small crew at the research station cannot leave, and no one new can arrive, until spring.
One winter, a cook at the station kept a journal about her months in the dark.
In the first weeks, she wrote, everything felt exciting: about forty people living together at the southern end of the Earth.
By June, however, her journal had changed.
She missed her family, green trees and the feeling of sunshine on her face.
Her video calls home were short, and after each one, the hallways of the station seemed even quieter.
Some evenings, she sat alone in the kitchen after everyone had gone to bed, listening to the hum of the heaters.
Then one night, a scientist knocked on the kitchen door and told her to put on her warmest clothes.
Outside, the sky above the white ice was full of moving light.
Wide green bands stretched from one side of the sky to the other, folding and unfolding slowly, with pale pink edges at the bottom.
This was the aurora australis, or southern lights, which appear when tiny particles from the Sun hit the air high above Earth.
She stood in the freezing air for only a few minutes, because that was all she could bear, and she did not say a single word.
After that night, she began to join the others for movie nights and card games instead of sitting alone.
In late September, the whole crew gathered at the windows to watch a thin orange line appear on the horizon.
When the first edge of the Sun finally rose, people cheered, hugged and pressed their hands against the glass.
The cook wrote that it was the most beautiful sunrise of her life, even though it was only a small orange edge above the ice.

passages.title: A Night with the Dinosaurs
sentences: Once a year, the Harbor Town museum lets a small group of students spend the night in its dinosaur hall.
This year, Ana and Maya were chosen from the science club, and they arrived on Friday evening with sleeping bags and flashlights.
At first, Ana was not sure she would enjoy it, because she cared much more about soccer than about old bones.
Then Dr. Bell, the museum's paleontologist, led the group on a flashlight tour, and Ana's opinion began to change.
Dr. Bell stopped beside a glass case and lifted out a fossil tooth as long as Ana's hand.
"This belonged to a Tyrannosaurus rex," she said. "You may hold it, but please be gentle."
Ana turned the heavy tooth over in her palm and ran her thumb along its tiny, jagged edges.
Then she asked question after question.
How did scientists know how old it was? What did the animal eat? Why were its arms so short?
Dr. Bell answered every one, and she smiled at how fast the questions came.
At ten o'clock, the lights went down, and everyone lay in rows of sleeping bags under the skeleton of a long-necked dinosaur.
Soon the room was full of slow, sleepy breathing, but Ana was still wide awake.
The hall was enormous and silent, and with everyone else asleep, she suddenly felt very far from home and very much by herself.
She missed her own bed and the sound of Ben's video game through the wall.
Then she heard a whisper beside her: "Are you awake too?"
It was Maya, propped up on one elbow, her face lit by the soft green glow of the exit sign.
The two girls lay on their backs and looked up.
Moonlight from the tall windows fell across the skeleton, and they could see every bone of its long neck and tail.
"It walked on this same planet," Maya whispered, "millions and millions of years ago."
Ana thought about the tooth she had held, and about all the years between those animals and her.
She did not feel lonely anymore, and she fell asleep still looking up at the bones.

steps.say: The question asks how Leo felt at the end. So I read the last sentences.
Leo threw his arms up and grinned. He yelled, "I did it!"
Arms up and a big grin show a good feeling.
He did a hard trick after many tries. The good feeling after you do something hard is called proud.
